title: Indrani's thread
hookLine: a queen ties a blessed thread on the king of the gods before battle; centuries later, strangers tie them in the street
carry: anyone can tie the thread of protection
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

lines: NOT ALWAYS A BROTHER AND SISTER.
A KING OF THE GODS AT WAR.
cards: Some of the stories about the protective thread aren't about a brother and a sister at all. There's a king of the gods, going out to a war he's losing, and his wife, who won't let him go empty-handed.
And much later, there's a province about to be split in two, where people walk into the street and tie threads on strangers.
The rakhi glittering on cardboard in shop windows each summer has a longer, stranger history than the sibling ritual alone.

teach.b: First, the king. A story told in the Bhavishya Purana, and repeated at many rakhi ceremonies, says that Indra, king of the gods, was being beaten by the demons.
His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, prepared a protective thread, blessed with sacred words, and tied it on his wrist on the full moon of Shravana. He went back into battle and won.
So here the thread is tied by a wife on a husband, before a fight. Second, the priests.

teach.h: A PRIEST TIES IT ON HIS PEOPLE.
teach.b: In many parts of India, on this same full moon, a family priest ties a protective thread on the wrists of the people he serves. The thread was never only one relationship.
It's a blessing you can put on anyone you want to keep safe. Third, closer to our time. In 1905, the British government divided the province of Bengal.
On the day the division took effect, the poet Rabindranath Tagore called on people to tie rakhis on one another, Hindus and Muslims alike, as a sign that the people of Bengal would not be split.
People walked through Calcutta tying threads on neighbors and strangers. A wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister.
That's the teaching inside the thread: raksha, protection, is a sacred promise tied with a prayer, and no one relationship owns it.

Anyone you'd keep safe can wear it. And that's the week. A butter thief, banana peels at Vidura's house, one Goddess in many forms, lamps for a divine guest, a boy dark as a rain cloud, a pillar with no end, and a thread.

how: On Raksha Bandhan sisters tie rakhis on brothers, and in many regions family priests tie protective threads on the people they serve; the thread is also tied between friends, cousins and neighbors as a sign of care.

o: a sacred thread a priest wears for life
a bracelet given as a birthday gift
a thread tied on as a promise of protection

games.q: who tied the thread — tap the pairs.
p: tied it on Indra before battle
ties it on the people he serves

s: the rakhi has only ever been tied by sisters on brothers
in the stories a wife ties it on Indra; priests tie it on their people; in 1905 strangers tied it on each other.
Tagore called for rakhis between Hindus and Muslims in 1905
when Bengal was divided, he asked people to tie threads as a sign they would not be split.
in the Indra story, the thread is tied after the battle is won
Indrani ties it before he goes back to fight, and then he wins.

games.q: it's 1905, and the government is splitting your province, Bengal, in two. what does Tagore ask people to do?
o: tie rakhis on one another, Hindus and Muslims alike.
games.why: he asks them to tie threads on each other. people walk through Calcutta tying rakhis on neighbors and strangers.

practice: Let a first face come, someone you'd protect, maybe the one from last time; then a second, someone who isn't family: a coworker going through something, a neighbor who lives alone, someone you disagree with.
Picture tying a thread on their wrist too, and say inside: I'd look out for you. Stay with both faces for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Rakhi. The thread of protection, tied by a wife, a priest, a stranger, a sister. Always holding a promise.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Hindi: raksha, protection, and bandhan, a tie or bond.

carryVoice: Your line: anyone can tie the thread of protection. It was never only for brothers. That's day ninety-one.

sources.ref: Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva (Indrani ties the raksha on Indra)
Rabindranath Tagore and the Raksha Bandhan of October 1905 (partition of Bengal)
rakshasutra tied by priests on the Shravana full moon (regional practice)
